source.title: Concurrent Adversarial Learning for Large-Batch Training
source.authors: Yong Liu; Xiangning Chen; Minhao Cheng; Cho-Jui Hsieh; Yang You

record.file_problem: Full paper text is supplied; no apparent truncation or garbling that prevents extraction.
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures training–test accuracy gaps under large-batch training and tests whether concurrent adversarial training changes those gaps; this is a different intervention from the claim versions’ listed conditions.
record.gate_note: Reports ImageNet ResNet-50 accuracy and generalization-gap comparisons for vanilla training, ConAdv, and ConAdv with AutoAug across batch sizes. Also reports AutoAug comparisons and adversarial perturbation sweeps, but those latter accuracy results are not separate direct tests of the claim versions listed. Throughput and training-time results do not measure the generalization gap.
record.test_reason: The study directly sweeps batch size and measures held-out ImageNet accuracy after a fixed 90 epochs, testing V5 with and without recipe adaptations. The extracted rows instead measure training–test accuracy gaps, which are not V5's batch-size penalty.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors conclude that ConAdv improves large-batch ImageNet training, reduces the training–test gap, and permits concurrent adversarial-example generation. At 96k, ConAdv achieves 75.3% and ConAdv plus AutoAug achieves 76.2%, exceeding the 75.9% MLPerf target only with AutoAug. These results do not demonstrate preservation of each recipe's own small-batch accuracy.
record.recipe_differences: Uses LARS, fixed 90-epoch ImageNet-1k ResNet-50 training, and adversarial training with one-step PGD; studies batch-size scaling and the effect of Concurrent Adversarial Learning rather than the versions’ listed interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: Batch size; AutoAug and its combination with ConAdv; adversarial perturbation value. Table 4 shows the gap comparison across batch sizes and augmentation conditions.

fits_no_version.finding: ConAdv reduces training–test accuracy gaps at each reported batch size, with or without AutoAug.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Concurrent adversarial training reduces the training–test accuracy gap relative to vanilla ResNet-50 training on ImageNet at matched batch sizes.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR), 2021; text labels the document Preprint.
record.problems: Only one architecture and dataset are used for the generalization-gap comparison. No uncertainty estimates are reported. The fixed 90-epoch schedule means the number of updates changes with batch size. The paper says the largest-batch vanilla model at 64k is below the 75.9% MLPerf accuracy baseline, so its omitted 64k training time is not reported; 96k maximum-speed resource comparison is also unavailable.
record.rows_left_out: No required claim-version outcomes omitted. Table 1 and Table 2 top-1 accuracy and Table 5 perturbation sweeps are not separate rows because they report accuracy rather than the training–test gap that V5 names; the central gap results are extracted from Table 4.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its coexistence with natural-label generalization.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under different tuning budgets.

Language models, other architectures and datasets, longer training, and controlled comparisons isolating learning-rate scaling, warmup, or normalization changes. The recipe already uses LARS, warmup, weight decay, and label smoothing.
Dropout and its interactions with dataset size, augmentation, and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware weight sharpness and its ranking of generalization gaps.
Removing memorized examples versus random examples.

missing.what: Add held-out accuracy rows across batch sizes for vanilla, AutoAug, DisAdv, ConAdv, and ConAdv plus AutoAug. Tables 1–2 are declared omitted, but the stated justification reverses V5's actual measure; these rows are required to capture the tested version and substantiate the text-based verdicts.

Add the extreme-batch accuracy results: vanilla versus AutoAug is 73.2% versus 72.9% at 128k and 64.7% versus 62.5% at 256k, compared with 76.9% versus 77.5% at 1k. These extend the batch-size scope beyond the record's stated 96k limit.

record.verdict_notes: No supplied original-source restriction applies. Smaller training–test gaps are not evidence that increasing batch size preserves test accuracy: vanilla's gap decreases from 5.9 points at 32k to 4.3 at 64k while test accuracy also decreases. No uncertainty estimates are supplied. The claimed ICLR 2021 publication status is not established by the supplied preprint.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence are not tested.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison.
No adaptive-optimizer versus SGD generalization comparison.
Tests ImageNet ResNet-50 under 90-epoch training with LARS. It does not test language models, batches beyond 96K, or the alternative recipe adaptations named in the version.
No magnitude-aware sharpness or other generalization-measure comparison.

relationships.condition: Vanilla ResNet-50 on ImageNet, LARS, fixed 90 epochs, batches above 32k
relationships.reason: Text-based verdict from Table 1; missing accuracy rows show 76.6% at 32k, 75.3% at 64k, and 74.3% at 96k.
relationships.display_finding: Vanilla accuracy decreased beyond batch 32k despite LARS, but these comparisons remain unverified.

relationships.condition: AutoAug, ConAdv, and ConAdv plus AutoAug, fixed 90 epochs, 32k–96k batches
relationships.reason: Text-based verdict from Tables 1–2: accuracy falls from 32k to 96k under every recipe, while ConAdv reduces the vanilla decline from 2.3 to 2.0 points and ConAdv plus AutoAug reduces it to 2.1 points.
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy declined with every augmentation recipe, and ConAdv modestly reduced the decline, but these comparisons remain unverified.

relationships.condition: Vanilla and AutoAug ResNet-50 at extreme batch sizes, fixed 90 epochs
relationships.reason: Text-based verdict from Section 3.1 and Figure 2: vanilla accuracy falls from 76.9% at 1k to 73.2% at 128k and 64.7% at 256k; AutoAug reaches only 72.9% and 62.5% at those extreme batches.
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy fell substantially at extreme batch sizes with vanilla training and AutoAug, but these comparisons remain unverified.
